title: Brothers Selling Brothers: Nehemiah Confronts Debt and Greed
summary: In the middle of the building work, ordinary families cry out that famine, royal taxes, and debt have forced them to mortgage their land and sell their children into slavery to wealthier Jews. Nehemiah angrily confronts the nobles and officials, calls a public assembly, and makes them swear to stop charging interest and to give back what they have taken. He then describes how, as governor for twelve years, he refused the food allowance he was entitled to so as not to burden the people.
story: Chapter 4 ended with the community armed against enemies outside the walls. Chapter 5 turns to a threat from inside, and in some ways a worse one. The restored community in Judah was meant to be a people living under God's law, a brotherhood of former exiles. Now some of its members are growing rich by driving others into poverty and bondage. The wall is worth little if the city it protects is built on injustice. The chapter interrupts the account of the building to show that Nehemiah's reform was social as well as physical, and it looks ahead to the covenant renewal of chapters 8 to 10, where the people will again promise to live by the law.
historical:
Judah under Persian rule was a small and mostly agricultural province. Verse 4 mentions the king's tax on fields and vineyards: the Persian Empire collected tribute from every province, often in silver, and a small farmer who had to pay in silver in a bad harvest year had little choice but to borrow. Verse 3 speaks of a famine, and verse 2 of large families needing grain. The builders' time on the wall may also have taken men away from their fields. The result was a familiar pattern in the ancient world: poor farmers pledged their land and finally their children to wealthy lenders.

Verse 14 gives the length of Nehemiah's first term as governor: from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes I, about 445 to 433 BC. This part of the chapter is written from a later vantage point, looking back over those twelve years. The earlier governors he mentions in verse 15 are not named here; the reference shows that Judah had governors before him, whose demands had been heavy.
cultural:
The law of Moses allowed lending but forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite who was poor (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20). It also allowed a poor Israelite to sell his labor to pay a debt, but it required that he be treated as a hired worker rather than a slave and released in the year of release (Leviticus 25:39-43; Deuteronomy 15:12-15). The complaint in this chapter is that these protections had broken down. Daughters were already in bondage, and families had no way to redeem them because their land, the only source of income, now belonged to the lenders.

Verse 11 mentions a percentage, literally the hundredth part, of money, grain, wine, and oil; many interpreters take this as an interest charge of one percent a month, though the exact meaning is uncertain. Nehemiah's gesture in verse 13 is a public sign-act: he shakes out the fold of his robe (a garment gathered at the waist could serve as a pocket) and pronounces a curse on anyone who breaks the oath. The assembly's “Amen” binds them to it. Verses 17-18 reflect the obligations of a Persian-era governor, who was expected to host officials and visitors at his table at great expense.
literary: The chapter has two parts. The first (verses 1-13) is a scene of complaint and response: three groups speak in turn (verses 2, 3, and 4-5), each describing a deeper stage of poverty, then Nehemiah reacts with anger, deliberates, confronts the leaders, calls an assembly, and secures an oath. The second part (verses 14-19) is a personal account, a kind of defense of his own conduct, contrasting him with the governors before him. The chapter ends with one of Nehemiah's short prayers asking God to remember him, a refrain that recurs in 13:14, 22, and 31 and gives the memoir its distinctive voice.

outline.t: The outcry of the poor: hunger, mortgages, taxes, and slavery
Nehemiah rebukes the nobles and demands restitution
An oath before the priests and a public curse

doctrines.note: The law of Moses protected the poor from interest and permanent bondage. Nehemiah's appeal is not to a new ideal but to the covenant they already had: “Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies?” (verse 9).

The whole community is spoken of as brothers (verses 1, 5, 7, 8). Economic exploitation is treated as a betrayal of family, and the cry of parents whose daughters are enslaved sets the chapter's moral weight.
Nehemiah twice grounds conduct in “the fear of God” (verses 9 and 15). Reverence for God is shown not first in ritual but in how the powerful treat the vulnerable.

words.note: Tseaqah, cry or outcry. The word often describes the cry of the oppressed that reaches God's ears, as in Israel's cry in Egypt (Exodus 3:7, 9). Placing it at the start of the chapter frames the complaint of the poor as the kind of cry God answers, and Nehemiah acts as God's responder.

Mashsha, interest or a loan on pledge. Nehemiah uses it for the practice the nobles were exacting from their brothers (verses 7 and 10). The term concerns lending that takes advantage of another's need, which the law forbade among Israelites.

Yirah, fear. In the Old Testament the fear of God is reverent awe that shapes behavior, the beginning of wisdom. Nehemiah uses it as the reason the nobles should stop (verse 9) and as the reason he himself refused the governor's allowance (verse 15).

Zakar, to remember. The closing prayer asks God to remember Nehemiah for good. This is not a claim to have earned salvation but a request that God take note of faithfulness done at personal cost, a theme that returns at the end of the book.

christ: The connection to Christ is thematic. Nehemiah sets aside his rights as governor so as not to burden the people and spends his own resources on their behalf. Paul describes Christ in similar terms, though on an infinitely greater scale: though he was rich, for our sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). The chapter's concern for the enslaved poor also belongs to the long biblical hope for release that Jesus claimed at Nazareth when he read from Isaiah about proclaiming liberty to captives (Luke 4:18-19). And the early church in Acts, where believers shared so that there was no needy person among them (Acts 4:34), shows the same brotherhood that Nehemiah tried to restore.

hard.q: Why does the Bible allow people to sell their children into servitude at all?
hard.a:
The chapter does not approve of what is happening; it presents the bondage of children as a crisis that Nehemiah is angry about and works to end. Still, readers rightly ask why the law of Moses permitted debt servitude in the first place. In the ancient Near East, when a family fell into debt with no land or goods left, selling labor was often the only alternative to starvation. The Mosaic law did not invent this practice but regulated it: it required that an Israelite in debt service be treated as a hired worker rather than a slave, limited the term, and commanded release with provisions (Leviticus 25:39-43; Deuteronomy 15:12-15). It also forbade interest to the poor, which was meant to keep families from falling into such debt at all.

Some interpreters see these laws as God meeting a harsh economy where it was and restraining its worst abuses, while pointing toward a fuller justice later revealed. Others emphasize that the laws, faithfully kept, would have made permanent poverty nearly impossible. In either reading, Nehemiah 5 shows how quickly the protections were ignored when they cost the wealthy something, and how the prophets and reformers treated such neglect as a sin against God.

questions: The poor in this chapter were exploited by their own people, not by foreigners. Where might a community of faith be comfortable with injustice among its own members?
Nehemiah gave up an allowance he was entitled to because “the burden on the people was so heavy”. What rights or privileges might you set aside for the sake of others?
Nehemiah acted in anger, but only “after serious thought”. What does this chapter teach about how to turn righteous anger into wise action?
